title: Repo-digest LLM regeneration has no rate limit, cooldown, or budget accounting
detail: RepoDigestCache.current() (packages/server/src/orchestrator/repoDigest.ts:158-168) is called synchronously from Orchestrator.orientationFor() on every dispatch() and resumeRun() call. Whenever the checkout's HEAD has moved since the cached digest was written, it fires a background LLM generation (generateRepoDigest — a full read-only Agent SDK turn that reads repo files, not a cheap completion). The only throttle is a single-flight `refreshing` boolean that prevents two generations from overlapping; there is no minimum interval between successive generations, no cap on how often HEAD is allowed to trigger a regeneration, and no config toggle to disable the feature (grepped packages/core/src/config.ts and .dispatch/config.yml — nothing references digest). Unlike every other LLM-driven path in this codebase, this call is never checked against orchestrator.maxBudgetUsd (that cap is only threaded into startAndRegister's executor options in dispatch()/resumeRun()/dispatchAuxRun()). In the exact scenario this codebase is built around — an EpicEngine auto-dispatching many tasks whose runs squash-merge into the main checkout via the merge queue, each merge advancing HEAD — every merge can trigger another full-repo-read LLM call with no operator control over frequency or cost.

title: Digest generation failures are silent — no ledger/UI surfacing, unlike the established degradation pattern
detail: RepoDigestCache.refresh()'s catch handler (packages/server/src/orchestrator/repoDigest.ts:187-191) only does `console.error` on a generation failure (missing CLI, model error, etc.), and retries silently on the next dispatch — forever, if the underlying cause doesn't clear. This codebase already has an established convention for exactly this situation: DepMapCache's `onDegrade` callback (wired in packages/server/src/index.ts around the depMapCache construction) writes a `kind: 'hazard'` LedgerStore entry when carto degrades, so the failure is visible to a human via the app, not just server logs. The new digest cache has no equivalent — an operator whose digest generation is persistently broken (e.g. bad API key, no CLI on PATH in the daemon's environment) has no way to discover why the '## Repo orientation' section never gets a repo map, short of reading dispatchd's stdout.

title: Non-empty concurrent-runs prompt text drops the 'check again later' caveat the empty case has
detail: orientation.ts's renderConcurrentRuns (packages/server/src/orchestrator/orientation.ts:304-324) explicitly tells the agent, when nobody else is running, to 'call run_list only if you need a fresher answer later in your work.' When runs ARE listed, that caveat disappears — prompt.ts's orientation-present branch (packages/server/src/orchestrator/prompt.ts:101-105) instead states flatly 'Concurrency is already reported above, so you do not need to open with `run_list`,' with no reminder that this is a point-in-time snapshot taken before the agent's very first turn (dispatch() collects concurrentRuns synchronously before startAndRegister). For a long-running task, this asymmetry nudges the agent to treat stale-by-design concurrency data as settled fact for the whole run, which is exactly the collision risk run_list exists to catch (a new run getting dispatched on an overlapping file mid-task).

title: Stop escalation is a flat wall-clock timer, not tied to whether the agent actually kept working
detail: The confirmed design (per the task's Activity log) is: "a stop auto-escalates to a hard cancel if the agent keeps calling tools past a timeout." scheduleStopEscalation (orchestrator.ts:1045) does not implement that condition — it arms a single setTimeout(STOP_ESCALATION_MS = 120_000) at the moment requestStop() is called, and unconditionally falls back to cancel() if the run is still non-terminal 2 minutes later, with no check on whether the agent has issued any NEW tool call since the stop (which canUseTool would have denied) versus still being legitimately mid-way through the ONE tool call that was already in flight when Stop was pressed — the exact call graceful stop explicitly promises not to abort (see the STOP_ESCALATION_MS doc comment: "the agent may legitimately be mid-tool-call (a long test run, a large edit) when Stop is pressed, and that call is exactly what a graceful stop promises not to abort"). If that one legitimate in-flight operation (a long test suite, a large refactor, a slow build) takes longer than 2 minutes, the escalation timer fires anyway and calls cancel(), which — unlike the graceful finish path — skips handleFinish's auto-commit and leaves whatever that operation produced uncommitted and discarded. This silently converts a well-behaved graceful stop into the same data-losing outcome as a hard Cancel, for the exact scenario the feature was designed to protect. Confirmed by reading scheduleStopEscalation's implementation directly; the only test covering this path (stop.test.ts's 'does not cancel a run that wound down before the window elapsed') exercises a stop that finishes quickly, not a single in-flight operation that legitimately outlives the window, so this gap has no test coverage either.

title: "Stopped" chip doesn't distinguish a clean graceful stop from an escalated hard cancel
detail: deriveStopControl (apps/desktop/src/lib/runState.ts:150) sets showStoppedChip purely from `!live && stopRequestedAt !== undefined`, with no check on which terminal state the run actually landed in. Because stopRequestedAt is set once and never cleared (per its own doc comment: "never cleared — a stop cannot be taken back, only escalated to a hard cancel"), a run that gets escalated to cancel() by scheduleStopEscalation (see the related finding) ends up with state 'cancelled' AND stopRequestedAt set, so RunDetailHeader renders the same 'Stopped' chip (tooltip: 'Stop requested at <time>') as a run that wound down cleanly and had its work auto-committed. The two outcomes are materially different for the user — one preserves the agent's work as reviewable, the other discards it exactly like pressing Cancel — but the header gives no visual signal of which one happened; only digging into the Activity log (which does log 'escalating to cancel') reveals the difference. Confirmed by reading deriveStopControl and RunDetailHeader.tsx directly; runState.test.ts's coverage for a terminal+stopRequestedAt run only exercises the 'finished' case, not 'cancelled'.
